Njord: data, model and benchmark analysis

A practical explanation of the current implementation and what the experiments establish.

English report · Updated 25 November 2026 · Our archived runs, Nils’s supplied results and inspected code

1. Data versions

We use the same scientific ocean data in two storage representations. The difference is when we select ocean points and assign them to ranks. A rank is a process controlling one GPU in these runs.

Version A: original full storeVersion B: prepared ocean shards
Stored spatial points61,200 rectangular grid cells, including land.42,348 valid ocean points in total; 42,348 / 21,174 / 10,587 per rank with 1 / 2 / 4 GPUs.
When selection happensThe original sample-building path materializes full-grid data, then selects ocean points.An offline tool selects ocean points and writes each rank’s store before the run. Sample building still happens during training.
What is preservedOcean values, global node IDs, normalization statistics, masks and target definitions. We do not compute separate normalization statistics for each GPU.
Relevant runs4981: original model, full store.5031: original model, one ocean shard. 4944 / 4949 / 4952: distributed implementation, 1 / 2 / 4 ranks.

1.1 How we built the benchmark dataset

We started with 31 daily snapshots from 1–31 January 2023, for both ocean and atmosphere. The preparation script writes that complete 31-step sequence 16 times—the original sequence plus 15 copies—into physical_repeat_16. This gives 31 × 16 = 496 stored time positions. It repeats the sequence, rather than repeating each individual day 16 times.

The script shifts timestamps forward continuously, from 1 January 2023 to 10 May 2024, and writes independent Zarr time chunks. The physical values and stored forcing values—including day-of-year features—repeat; static fields, masks and normalization statistics are retained. These are 16 copies of a 31-day block, not 16 independent observed months. The purpose is a larger physical-data I/O benchmark, not additional scientific training data.

1.2 How we built Version B

Starting from this full repeated store, we apply the existing surface-ocean mask: 61,200 cells → 42,348 ocean points. Geographic RCB assigns each ocean point to one rank. We then write a paired ocean.zarr and atmosphere.zarr for every rank, with the source values, masks and statistics for its points.

Within one layout, each ocean point has exactly one owner. We preserve its original full-grid ID and ocean-node ID alongside a local contiguous index. The build validates source-value equality, coordinate alignment and complete, disjoint ownership. Halo feature copies are exchanged during model execution; they are not extra ocean points permanently duplicated in these shards.

What is saved, and how the time split is handled

Each layout contains manifest.json, surface_owners.npy and rank_0/, rank_1/, etc. Each rank directory contains its two Zarr stores. Coordinates global_grid_index and global_surface_index map local positions back to the source and graph. Time chunks contain one timestamp and all locally owned points.

The repeat builder keeps the original validation/test lengths (8 and 9 time positions), puts them at the end of the new timeline and uses the remaining 479 positions for training. The configured AR4 dataset yields 473 usable training windows. Original normalization statistics are copied rather than recomputed over the expanded timeline. Repeated patterns and artificial block boundaries mean these splits are suitable for this performance proxy, not independent forecast-skill evidence.

Where work happens when a run loads a batch

Original path:

Full Zarr chunks61,200 cells / time→Decode, normalize,
construct sample→Ocean selection,
masks + ice channel→Ocean batch → GPU

Prepared-shard path:

Offline: select ocean
and owner IDs once→Write rank stores→During run: decode,
normalize, build sample→Owned batch → GPU

The original source is already training-ready Zarr, rather than raw observations. Preparing shards changes the storage layout; it does not replace the remaining loader transformations or preload the whole dataset into memory.

Data contents, sample sizes and Zarr chunks

There are 27 physical state variables: sea-surface height; ice concentration and thickness; temperature, salinity and two current components at six depths. A derived binary ice-presence channel makes 28 model state channels.

Seven static features describe bathymetry, mean dynamic topography, coast distance and sine/cosine encodings of longitude and latitude. Two cyclic time features and eight atmospheric variables are windowed over three times, yielding six and 24 channels per forecast step.

For global batch size two, histories have shape [2, 2, N, 28] and targets [2, 4, N, 28]. Here N is the local number of ocean points. The condition has 2×28 + 6 + 7 + 24 = 93 channels per point. All effective model inputs are float32.

The original state chunks are [27 features, 1 time, 61200 cells] in float64; atmospheric chunks are [8, 1, 61200] in float32. Indexing a few cells may still decode the whole spatial chunk. Shards store the complete local spatial extent per time.

1.4 Workers, prefetch and temporary storage

Current AR4 runs use 8 workers per rank and prefetch 2: 8 / 16 / 32 workers in total on 1 / 2 / 4 GPUs. Prefetch 2 permits up to two pending batches per worker. More queue slots do not by themselves make decoding faster.

CPU workers prepare batch n+1while GPU computes batch n→Trainer receives CPU batch→Copy to GPU and wait→Wait for other ranks;
start next graph step

Workers use spawn and persist between batches. In the measured path, pin_memory=False; copies use non_blocking=True followed by a CUDA wait. CPU preparation can overlap compute, but GPU copies are not a double-buffered pipeline here.

Four different operations: staging copies compressed files to job-local $TMPDIR; spatial preprocessing writes a new layout; worker prefetch prepares future batches; RAM preload keeps decoded values resident. In these single-node jobs, ranks share a job staging root—GPUs do not each have their own temporary disk.

All ranks process the same dates and global batch of two. They own different places, not different samples. The loader and graph must use the same global node IDs and ownership plan.

2. Model: where message passing happens, before and now

The original model already performs graph message passing. Our implementation distributes those same graph operations across spatial partitions and adds communication when a receiver needs a sender owned by another rank.

PartBefore: original GraphEFMNow: distributed execution
Graph and learned transformationsGrid, two meshes, edge MLPs and node MLPs execute on one GPU.Same topology, formulas and model complexity. Nodes and receiver-owned edges are partitioned.
Sender featuresEvery sender is already on the device.Local senders are available; remote sender features arrive as temporary halo copies.
AggregationCombine all incoming edge messages for each receiver.The receiver owner still holds all incoming edges and performs the same complete mean or sum.
Autoregressive feedbackKeep the complete predicted ocean state on one GPU.Each rank keeps its own predicted state for the next step. No full-grid gather between forecasts.
BackwardOrdinary autograd; checkpointing recomputes activations.Also return halo gradients to sender owners and sum gradients for replicated model weights. Replay must use a consistent communication schedule.

2.1 One training forecast, in execution order

The two grid MLPs assemble representations before graph processing. History-only inputs have 93 channels; adding the target’s 28 channels creates a separate 121-channel posterior input. Both are embedded to width 64. Coarser meshes have fewer nodes, but still 64 features per node.

A. Posterior: target-aware path · 4 graph applications
121 → 64 MLP→Grid → mesh 0mean→Mesh 0 ×1sum→Up to mesh 1mean→Mesh 1 ×1sum→q(μ, σ) → sample z
B. Decoder: its own traversal using history and z · 10 graph applications
History embedding→Grid → mesh 0mean→Mesh 0 ×2sum→Up to mesh 1sum; receiver starts from MLP(z)→Mesh 1 ×2sum→Down to mesh 0mean; saved fine states→Mesh 0 ×2sum→Mesh → gridsum; grid skip path→64 → 28 MLPstate increment
C. Prior: history-only path for the KL term · 4 graph applications
93 → 64 MLPembedding shared with decoder→Grid → mesh 0mean→Mesh 0 ×1sum→Up to mesh 1mean→Mesh 1 ×1sum→p(μ, σ = 1)

Training uses 18 graph applications per forecast and 72 across AR4. Each branch sends fine information upward once, then performs its coarse layers; it does not resend mesh 0 before every mesh-1 layer. The decoder receives the sampled latent z rather than continuing the posterior’s hidden mesh states.

Inference: history → prior → sample z → decoder → prediction. There is no target or posterior: 14 graph applications per forecast, 56 across four steps per ensemble member. Different latent draws produce different scenarios.

MLPs, aggregation formulas and residual connections

Grid condition MLP: 93 → 64 → 64; posterior grid MLP: 121 → 64 → 64. Separate mesh and edge geometry MLPs use 4 → 64 → 64. After G2M, each branch applies a pointwise SiLU + Linear 64 → 64 projection.

For every edge, concatenate [edge(64), sender(64), receiver(64)]. The edge MLP is 192 → 64 → 64; after aggregation, the receiver-update MLP is 128 → 64 → 64.

Propagation: G2M, encoder/prior up, decoder down
m = h_sender + EdgeMLP([e, h_sender, h_receiver])
a = mean(all incoming m)
h_receiver_new = a + NodeMLP([h_receiver, a])
Interaction: within meshes and decoder up
m = EdgeMLP([e, h_sender, h_receiver])
a = sum(all incoming m)
h_receiver_new = h_receiver + NodeMLP([h_receiver, a])

Within-mesh layers also return e_new = e + m. These updated edges feed later layers; saved fine states and edges are reused on descent. Cross-level edge embeddings are not updated. M2G uses the interaction-style sum and receiver residual without updating edges.

The decoder embeds z with 64 → 64 → 64, builds a grid skip h + MLP(h), applies a 64 → 64 projection before M2G and a final 64 → 64 → 28 increment map. Standard hidden MLPs use Linear → SiLU → Linear → LayerNorm; distribution and final-output maps omit the last LayerNorm.

2.3 How a message crosses the GPU boundary

  1. Gather: select unique remote sender IDs with index_select and pack their current features.
  2. Send / receive: post grouped isend / irecv operations with batch_isend_irecv, then wait for completion. Peer transfers can run concurrently.
  3. Compute locally: concatenate owned and halo sender states, run the edge MLP for each local receiver edge, aggregate all messages, then update receivers.
  4. Return gradients: autograd sums uses of a halo copy, sends its gradient to the owner, and the owner adds it with index_add.
  5. Synchronize weights: sum replicated parameter gradients with all_reduce(SUM) before AdamW. Spatial contributions are summed, not averaged over ranks.

For batch size 2, width 64 and float32, one distinct remote sender costs 512 feature bytes per peer per exchange, before protocol overhead. Current code waits for halos before the graph operator; useful local edge computation is not yet deliberately overlapped with those transfers.

Topology, real partitions, latent distributions and training loss

Graph creation uses coordinates rather than the 93 physical-input channels. The cluster builder forms mesh 0 with spherical K-means and forms the next level from preceding mesh positions. Spherical Delaunay gives candidate same-level edges, followed by configured filters. G2M uses a radius neighbourhood; the builder default is 0.67 × mean fine-mesh chord-edge length, a chosen hyperparameter. M2G selects nearest mesh nodes (requested degree three); fine-to-coarse links choose a nearest coarse node and reverse for descent. The benchmark loads saved graph files; their exact generation command is not recorded.

The measured geographic RCB baseline balances each layer independently: south/north for two ranks, then an unwrapped-longitude split at four. It is not the older fixed −5° cut. Equal grid counts do not imply equal mesh/edge/halo cost.

The posterior predicts a diagonal Gaussian on 2,097 coarse nodes, with 64 means and 64 scales per node; scales are softplus(raw) + 10⁻⁴. The prior learns means and fixes standard deviation to one in this configuration. Sampling occurs after the encoder’s messages; it does not replace aggregation.

The objective is weighted reconstruction error + β·KL(q||p), with β = 1 and CRPS weight zero. It sums time, spatial and feature/latent contributions and averages the batch. Output constraints and ice-density feedback are applied before using predictions as later history. The four forecasts are connected without detaching.

MP checkpoint replay executes another 72 forward graph applications in backward, plus reverse halo gradients. Early stopping is disabled in MP so ranks replay a consistent communication schedule; the original reference enables it. Latent noise is drawn outside replay and selected by global coarse-node IDs. Full scenario inference throughput is not measured here.

3.1 What did the data control change?

4981 → 5031: the original model improves from 1.062 to 1.197 samples/s when using the prepared ocean store: +12.8% observed throughput. 5031 → MP1: the remaining difference is +4.1%, rather than the earlier +17.5% comparison against the full-store reference.

A data-layout change can also affect forward/backward intervals: background CPU preparation competes with the training process, and event intervals can include launch gaps. The remaining one-GPU difference is not an isolated implementation gain: checkpoint replay and preflight-batch lifetime still differ, and there is only one independent job per case.

3.2 Where is the time spent now?

Visible input accounts for about 6.3% of original/full, 5.5% of original/ocean and 2–4% of MP time.

data_read_ms measures the trainer’s wait for the CPU batch, including preparation when it is not already prefetched. host_to_device_ms covers copying and waiting. data_rank_wait_ms covers rank readiness. Graph halo traffic is inside forward/backward, rather than these loading timers. A small visible wait does not mean CPU decoding was free.

MP2 → MP4: mean batch time increases by about 78 ms. On the additive critical-rank timeline this is mainly +63 ms backward, +12 ms forward and +7 ms weight synchronization, partly offset by 8 ms less input time. This identifies where to investigate; it does not prove whether packing, CPU scheduling, small kernels, replay or imbalance dominates.

3.3 Throughput, memory and correctness

Relative to MP1, two GPUs achieve 1.353× speedup and 67.6% efficiency; four achieve 1.269× and 31.7%. MP2 is fastest at this model size. MP4 reduces memory per GPU to 0.965 GiB, despite taking longer per batch.

Allocated GPU-seconds/sample are 0.802 / 1.186 / 2.529 for MP1 / MP2 / MP4, excluding startup. Thus MP2 favors latency, while MP1 favors GPU-time efficiency at H64. This is not a billing formula.

The 50 measured scalar losses are exactly equal for original/full, original/ocean and MP1. Maximum relative deviations are 2.18×10⁻⁷ for MP2 and 1.82×10⁻⁷ for MP4. Small-graph CUDA/NCCL tests additionally compare predictions, gradients and optimizer updates. This is strong implementation evidence, rather than a long-horizon scientific skill assessment.

Published multi-rank phase means maximize each phase independently across ranks. Do not sum them: different maxima can come from different ranks, and compute/step/end-to-end are nested intervals. The stacked plot instead uses one critical-rank record per step.

All five current runs used the same node and GPU model, but separate allocations and physical GPU UUIDs. There are no independent repetitions yet. Staging, initialization and cache construction are excluded from steady-state throughput; 5031 stages both original metadata/source and its shard.

The MP runner keeps the preflight batch alive during measurement, while the original runner replaces it. One global batch is about 93 MiB; MP1’s peak is about 89 MiB higher than the original’s. This is a relevant buffer-lifetime difference, not an exact allocation attribution.

3.4 Combined findings with Nils’s PhysicsNeMo results

Spatial distribution reduces memory in both implementations. Nils also demonstrates substantially better four-GPU scaling in his experiment, especially at H128/H256. The new evidence comes from slides 2–7 of pnemo-results.pptx, supplied on 25 November. Values below preserve the rounded slide labels. The raw Package E archive is still unavailable here, so no independent reanalysis of its confidence intervals or profiler traces is claimed.

These are independent experiments. Same AR4 architecture settings and GPU model do not make them a controlled backend comparison. The mesh, deterministic policy, input activity, samples, checkpoint baseline and statistics differ. Each speedup uses its own reference.

Input wait alone does not explain the gap. Our H64 model interval is 1,540 / 1,146 / 1,232 ms on 1 / 2 / 4 GPUs, giving 1.345× and 1.251× model-interval speedups. Removing the visible 2–4% input phase therefore leaves the four-GPU slowdown in place. Background CPU contention can still inflate model intervals even when the next batch is already ready. Cached timing removes that worker activity as well as exposed input time.

The committed Nils ownership map confirms 7,193 / 1,812 mesh nodes, versus 8,456 / 2,097 in our result metadata. Recreate ownership on the chosen common graph before reusing a partition. Both paths retain the original edge/node MLP formulas and exchange complete required sender features. PhysicsNeMo’s exact graph exchange does not establish that PyG itself requires neighbour sampling: our PyG operators also use all assigned edges.

Our model interval is a CUDA-event mean from a live run; Nils’s main cached step is a synchronized wall-time median. Both include training work and communication, but they are not identical metrics. His live cases also change original full-store input at K=1 to rank files at K>1.

The deck’s counts differ by about 71× between chunks and Mt-KaHyPar. These are halo counts, not measured training-time ratios. The slides do not give the corresponding chunk-runtime comparison.

For four-GPU METIS, weighting reduces grid-node max/mean imbalance from 1.336 to 1.016, while mesh-0 imbalance rises from 1.007 to 1.082 and mesh-1 from 1.009 to 1.066. Weighted METIS/Mt-KaHyPar give a reported 2–4% step-time gain on two GPUs; the deck reports no significant difference on four under its CI criterion. Optimizing a structural count helps define candidates, but runtime remains the decision metric.

Nils’s framework uses indexed all-to-all; ours posts neighbour P2P operations. Both send selected feature rows and return their gradients. Neither implementation deliberately overlaps local edge compute with halo exchange. NCCL kernel durations can include rank waiting, and his explicit halo timers cover forward/replay, rather than the complete reverse-gradient exchange.

What the combined evidence supports

  • Demonstrated: both implementations reduce per-GPU memory substantially; four GPUs can unlock execution choices that one GPU cannot fit.
  • Demonstrated within Nils’s setup: four-GPU scaling improves with width; H128 reaches 3.42× over one GPU and H256 reaches 1.93× from two to four. Wider cases have only one launch and do not assess forecast accuracy.
  • Demonstrated within our setup: MP2 is faster than MP4 at H64, and excluding visible input does not remove that result.
  • Still a hypothesis: which part of the gap comes from transport, deterministic kernels, graph/ownership, CPU scheduling or the adapter. The slides do not isolate these causes.

3.5 CPU placement and the controlled transport results

Latest evidence: jobs 6114, 6117, 6121 and 6131, pulled at 8554302. The large improvement is a setup-level change affecting both backends. A smaller PhysicsNeMo advantage remains within matched pairs. The older live-input AR4 tables above are historical experiments, not the latest scaling curve.

The official statistic is the ratio of medians of three per-launch step medians. Each launch has 10 warmup and 50 measured updates per backend. Inputs are four pre-built CPU batches; Zarr reading, H2D and pre-step barriers are outside this timer. Forecasts, loss, gradients and two unmasked AdamW updates pass the paired equivalence gate.

Observed setup change: P2P 1,974.17 → 759.45 ms (2.60×); PN 1,805.69 → 734.87 ms (2.46×). Both improve substantially. Model configuration, graph, partition, weights, exact cached input hashes, deterministic policy and checkpoint replay match. The setup also changed launch method, CPU placement, OpenMP affinity policy and node/topology. Under the user's assumption of negligible node performance differences, CPU/startup placement is the leading explanation; this is not an isolated fixed-pair experiment.

Most of the reduction lies in forward and backward, where host launch delays and halo waits are included. The median optimizer interval across all ranks falls from 19.05 to 6.81 ms for P2P and from 18.87 to 0.67 ms for PN. The parameter set is unchanged. These intervals are not kernel-only measurements, so this does not prove an optimizer arithmetic optimization.

Why does CPU placement matter, and is fixed pinning necessary?

There are three separate decisions: Slurm reserves CPUs, a process/thread has an allowed affinity mask, and the OS schedules that thread within its mask. Our job contains one Slurm task; torchrun creates four child ranks inside it. Slurm does not automatically assign distinct CPU pairs to those children. Linux children inherit affinity across fork/exec. With a healthy shared eight-CPU mask, fixed pairs need not be required. With all four main threads restricted to the same two CPUs, unused reserved capacity cannot help them.

The requirement is sufficient effective CPU capacity. Disjoint pairs are our explicit, reproducible policy, not a mathematical requirement of GraphEFM or PhysicsNeMo. GPU kernel dispatch, packing and communication progress still need host execution even with zero DataLoader workers. Delayed ranks can make other ranks wait repeatedly during AR4 and checkpoint replay.

New trace fact: batch entry and the srun launcher already see CPUs 10–17. The only mask change in all 12 rank reports is our initial placement before importing torch. No later recorded checkpoint repairs a mask after imports, thread setup, CUDA/NCCL, cache setup or warmup. This supports simplifying the eventual implementation to placement plus verification. It does not establish which component narrowed job 6121, whose pre-init masks were never captured.

A version-specific NCCL lead and the missing causal test

The package archive lists nvidia-nccl-cu12==2.29.3. In the corresponding upstream initTransportsRank source, the original affinity is saved, GPU-local affinity is applied, and the exit path applies comm->cpuAffinity again instead of the saved value. That is a concrete mechanism capable of retaining a narrow mask in the executing thread. Group initialization can execute work in the caller. This matches the kind of symptom seen in 6121, but the actually loaded NCCL version and pre/post-init masks must be measured before calling it the proven cause.

Our initialization passes device_id and eagerly connects NCCL. Nils initializes without that argument and then calls a barrier. The invocation/thread path and the intersection of allocated CPUs with GPU-local CPUs may therefore matter. The 6131 allocation is entirely on CPU NUMA node 1 while the GPUs report node 0; no later automatic narrowing was observed. This is a topology-specific hypothesis, not proof that NCCL or Slurm is universally broken.

A short probe should record batch/worker masks before imports, after thread setup, after CUDA setup, after eager or lazy NCCL creation and after the first collective; also record torch.cuda.nccl.version() and per-thread masks. Run eager/lazy cases in fresh processes within the same allocation. Separately compare a shared full CPU pool with disjoint pairs under the same allocation. These tests distinguish inherited/startup narrowing, NCCL behavior and the necessity of fixed pairs.

Why does Nils not need our workaround?

His code does not contain a special CPU-affinity fix either. Both use torchrun, NCCL and one PyTorch CPU compute thread per rank. Nils records initial_affinity and cpu_affinity, but his raw metadata is not committed, so his actual allocation and masks remain unknown. A healthy inherited mask could make explicit pinning unnecessary. PhysicsNeMo does not automatically fix our host allocation: both candidates in job 6121 shared the same restricted masks.

The original global-model training enables deterministic algorithms and has no explicit per-rank CPU pinning. Our archived original-model job 5031 had a normal two-CPU mask for one GPU. Nils also differs in graph size, ownership inheritance, compact CSC layout, deterministic policy, distribution-argument checks and one-GPU reference. His requirements pin the same Torch/CUDA wheel as ours; a different loaded CUDA module alone is not evidence of a different Torch runtime. His 2.42× H64 scaling and our backend ratios answer different questions.

Does PhysicsNeMo still help when CPU placement is the same?

Yes, a small advantage is observed in all three new matched pairs. Both candidates use exactly the same CPU masks. The reported throughput gain is 3.34%, equivalent to 3.24% less step time. Its archived paired-launch bootstrap ratio interval is [1.0151, 1.1011], based on only three independent pairs.

The median of the three individual paired gains is 1.89%; this differs from the published ratio-of-medians estimator. The PN-first launch has the largest gain, so order/carryover remains a candidate explanation for part of the variation. The 14.4% smoke result is not a steady-state result. Evidence supports a modest, workload-specific transport benefit, not a universal 2–3× PhysicsNeMo gain.

What should be cleaned up after the reference is fixed?

  1. Centralize the workload and CPU policy; preserve the same reference configuration and recorded hashes.
  2. Keep CPU/Slurm setup in the launcher. After a same-allocation placement test, prefer one initial placement plus assertions over repeated blanket helper-thread repairs. No later repair was needed in 6131.
  3. Keep one training/timing pipeline with a selectable halo transport. The current global monkeypatch is useful for this experiment, but an explicit interface would make future maintenance clearer.
  4. Audit the duplicated distributed training flow against original GraphEFM before considering Nils's original-layer wrapper as a replacement. Model-source identity alone does not prove every distributed training detail.
  5. Separate original-reference, cached-transport and live-input experiments. Retain raw archives and compact provenance; reduce duplicate reporting, not evidence.

Next evidence, in order: retrieve Nils's initial/post-init affinity and runtime metadata; run the short eager/lazy placement probe; decide whether fixed pairs are needed; then collect matching one-/two-GPU references under the chosen policy. If the small backend difference matters, use at least four counterbalanced paired launches before making it a design decision. Change deterministic/distribution-validation policy only in separately labelled tests. Code cleanup follows this stable experiment definition; it is not itself a performance claim.

3.6 Exploratory AR1 tests — historical context only

The earlier one-step runs were useful for checking communication and exploring loaders, workers and prefetching. AR1 is too light to represent our target AR4 training workload: it unrolls one forecast instead of four, reducing autoregressive compute, activation and replay work. This does not necessarily mean a different spatial architecture.

In that lighter setup, visible input could take roughly 90% of a step; more workers helped some configurations and hurt others. These are interesting engineering observations, but they are not used to judge the full model’s scaling or select its final loader settings. The performance conclusions and next steps above are based on the current AR4 series.

On one GPU, moving from zero to two workers reduced visible input from 1,411 to 486 ms, while the model step changed only slightly: 224 → 221 ms. On four GPUs, the two-worker run was slower in both input (1,085 → 2,174 ms) and model-step time (117 → 831 ms). This is consistent with host-side contention or scheduling effects, but these timers alone do not establish the cause.

All six jobs used the same node and 238 measured AR1 steps. Workers are per rank; the two-worker runs use prefetch 2. These are separate historical jobs, not independent repetitions of a controlled worker experiment. The additive plots use one critical-rank record per step, so components can differ from the archive’s independently maximized phase means. “Data time” is visible input wait/copy/distribution, not all background CPU work; “model time” is elapsed step time, not pure GPU arithmetic.

Branch update checked 24 November 2026: only Alex’s branch advanced since the previous snapshot, from 9f058a3 to 5beb952. The initial overlap runs failed with OOM; a checkpoint/autograd fix now lets H64 overlap training complete on two and four GPUs. CPU/Gloo and CUDA/NCCL equivalence checks passed. It saves peak memory, while the matched timing pairs show lower throughput.

New Alex overlap results and their relevance

2 GPUs: 0.558 → 0.498 samples/s (-10.7%), and 2.80 → 2.38 GiB/GPU (-15.3%). 4 GPUs: 0.489 → 0.446 samples/s (-8.7%), and 2.43 → 2.24 GiB/GPU (-7.9%).

The old nested edge-gradient calls could trigger repeated full autoregressive checkpoint replay. The fix unpacks checkpoint inputs in the outer backward and rebuilds local/remote edge MLP graphs. A regression test checks exactly one replay per checkpointed forecast step.

Each timing pair used the same node/cards, 20 warmup + 200 measured steps, H64/L2/B2/AR4 and zero loader workers. There is one matched pair per GPU count; absolute rates are not a controlled comparison with our eight-worker, rank-local path. The raw JSON records a dirty worktree containing the fix, which was later committed as a69138e. The new launcher defaults are shorter (10 warmup + 40 measured), rather than the counts used for these archived results.

Pinned benchmark report and raw results. For our next steps: check replay correctness and profile before assuming communication overlap will improve speed.

Alex partitions mesh processing while keeping grid/G2M/M2G work replicated; our current path partitions these as well. These are alternative runtime boundaries, so integration needs an explicit choice rather than simply combining both implementations.

The earlier Lassi/Nils rows describe the pinned branch review through 24 November; they are not a claim about every newer branch. The new nils-pnemo row reflects the 25 November inspection and supplied slides. Nils’s October profiling used another GPU; his new PhysicsNeMo results use the same GTX 1080 Ti GPU model as ours, but a different mesh and benchmark policy.

4.2 When to revisit loading and model size

After one ownership interface exists, compare shared CPU reading, direct indexed reading and validated derived caches at a fixed CPU budget. Every backend must return identical local tensors. Record cache construction and staging separately as well as steady-state throughput. Current all-grid chunks make repeated independent decoding a real risk.

Run separately labelled width and checkpoint sweeps to find the scaling and capacity crossover. Nils’s wider cases now provide a reason to test this, with independent repetitions still needed. A larger model changes compute-to-communication balance and may hide input preparation; it does not by itself repair an inefficient pipeline or establish better forecast accuracy.
